name: Advanced Seminar Innovation & Entrepreneurship: Current Issues in Technology Management
description:
"Who Wins and Who Loses from Innovation?"

Thriving businesses are those that anticipate and adapt to rapid technological change and innovate. Against this backdrop, managers need to understand two sets of issues covered in this course.

(i)	IP and Patents Licensing 
In 2020, the automotive industry was shaken when courts blocked Daimler from selling cars over patent disputes with tech giants like Nokia and Sharp. Similar battles extend across industries: Apple and Qualcomm frequently clashed over wireless patents, while AI-generated inventions like DABUS challenge traditional patent laws. With industries from telecommunications to pharmaceuticals sometimes navigating tens of thousands of patents to bring products to market, the role of patents, licensing, and innovation strategies has never been more critical.

(ii)	AI Business Models
Beyond new discoveries, AI enables new ways of doing business. Predictive AI technologies sparked a shift in value capture from pipeline to platform businesses, which focus on ecosystem orchestration. Generative and agentic AI are now opening up another whole world of possibilities affecting all areas. For example, in education, institutions like Harvard have begun offering courses delivered by AI-generated digital twins of their professors, while companies more broadly are pushing toward high profitability with minimal headcount, running lean, agentic organizations instead of traditional teams. At the same time, the social and environmental costs of these business models must be better understood.

This seminar gives an understanding of the research toolbox and prepares you for your Master's thesis. You will choose a topic in the area of (i) IP, Licensing, and Innovation or (ii) strategic, economic, social or environmental implications of AI in business. You will develop a research question that you seek to answer in your seminar paper. You will write a seminar paper, present your work in class, and you will discuss a fellow student's seminar paper.

More specifically, you will practice relevant skills for your Master's thesis. These skills include, among others: spotting and framing an interesting phenomenon, identifying the relevant conversation in the literature, critically reviewing the literature, practicing empirical methods of research (qualitative or quantitative), and reflecting on your own work. You will practice scientific writing, presenting, and discussing. This work will deepen your knowledge of innovation management in general and attain specialist knowledge on their selected topic.

Example topics include:
- Patent Licensing Strategies and Firm Innovation
- Can AI Be an Inventor? The Patentability of AI-Generated Inventions
- Future Trends of AI and Patent Analytics
- The Role of Standard Essential Patents in the Current Innovation Ecosystem
- Patent Litigation and its Effect on Innovation
- Digital and AI Sustainability
- AI for Business Strategy Formulation or Implementation

To support research in the IP area, the seminar will provide exclusive access to PATSTAT, a leading global patent database. This will allow you to work with real-world patent data and gain hands-on experience in analyzing patenting trends and innovation dynamics.

You may also choose to work with other existing datasets or collect your own data, depending on what is appropriate for your question.
prerequisites:
Basic knowledge in technology and innovation management is recommended, e.g. through courses such as
- Technology and Innovation Management: Introduction
- Advanced Technology and Innovation Management

Optional (but highly recommended for quantitative projects): Proficiency in statistical analysis (using R, SPSS, or Stata) and data handling (e.g., MySQL and Python)

You must be curious about asking questions and solving them through the scientific method.
